claim: The ABCD study included 7512 participants (3625 [48.3%] females, aged 9.91 ± 0.62 y) who provided self-reported number of close friends, mental health and cognitive measures, and quality-controlled MRI data at baseline.
source: In the ABCD study, 7512 participants (3625 [48.3%] females, aged 9.91 ± 0.62 y) provided self-reported number of close friends, a broad range of mental health and cognitive measures, and quality-controlled MRI data at baseline (Table 1)
evidence: The manuscript directly reports demographic and sample characteristics from the ABCD study dataset.

claim: 4290 participants (2044 [47.7%] females, aged 11.49 ± 0.66 y) had 2-year follow-up data available in the ABCD study.
source: 4290 of them (2044 [47.7%] females, aged 11.49 ± 0.66 y) had 2-year follow-up data available (Table 2)
evidence: The manuscript directly reports longitudinal follow-up sample characteristics.

claim: The social network dataset included 16,065 subjects from 48 middle schools (8065 [50.3%] female, aged 12.00 ± 1.03 y) who had complete key variables.
source: In the social network dataset, 16,065 subjects from 48 middle schools (8065 [50.3%] female, aged 12.00 ± 1.03 y) who had complete key variables were included (Table 3)
evidence: The manuscript directly reports demographic characteristics from the social network dataset.

claim: The number of close friends was significantly associated with 12 out of 20 mental health measures at baseline in the ABCD study.
source: The number of close friends was significantly associated with 12 out of 20 mental health measures, and 7 out of 10 cognitive scores at baseline (the total F-value of the linear and quadratic terms, p<0.05/30; Figure 2a–g)
evidence: Statistical analysis results are reported with specific p-value thresholds and referenced to figures showing the data.

claim: The number of close friends was significantly associated with 7 out of 10 cognitive scores at baseline in the ABCD study.
source: The number of close friends was significantly associated with 12 out of 20 mental health measures, and 7 out of 10 cognitive scores at baseline (the total F-value of the linear and quadratic terms, p<0.05/30; Figure 2a–g)
evidence: Statistical analysis results are reported with specific p-value thresholds and referenced to figures showing the data.

claim: For 18 outcomes except withdrawn/depressed, all quadratic terms reached significance after Bonferroni corrections (p<0.05/60).
source: For these 18 outcomes except the withdrawn/depressed, all quadratic terms reached significance after Bonferroni corrections (p<0.05/60)
evidence: Statistical significance is reported with specific correction methods and thresholds.

claim: All quadratic models provided a significantly better fit than the corresponding linear models (F = [13.25, 55.53], all p<0.001).
source: all quadratic models provided a significantly better fit than the corresponding linear models (F = [13.25, 55.53], all p<0.001)
evidence: Model comparison statistics are directly reported with F-values and p-values.

claim: The greatest effect sizes of the quadratic terms for mental health were observed for social problems (β = 0.08, t = 5.92, p=3.3 × 10–9, ΔR2 = 0.43%).
source: For mental health, the greatest effect sizes of the quadratic terms were observed for social problems (β = 0.08, t = 5.92, p=3.3 × 10–9, ΔR2 = 0.43%)
evidence: Statistical results including beta coefficients, t-values, p-values, and effect sizes are directly reported.

claim: The greatest effect sizes of the quadratic terms for mental health were observed for attention problems (β = 0.12, t = 5.83, p = 5.8 × 10–9, ΔR2 = 0.42%).
source: For mental health, the greatest effect sizes of the quadratic terms were observed for social problems (β = 0.08, t = 5.92, p=3.3 × 10–9, ΔR2 = 0.43%) and attention problems (β = 0.12, t = 5.83, p = 5.8 × 10–9, ΔR2 = 0.42%)
evidence: Statistical results including beta coefficients, t-values, p-values, and effect sizes are directly reported.

claim: The greatest effect sizes of the quadratic terms for cognition were observed for total intelligence (β = –0.35, t = –7.45, p=1.0 × 10–13, ΔR2 = 0.50%).
source: For cognition, the greatest effect sizes of the quadratic terms were observed for total intelligence (β = –0.35, t = –7.45, p=1.0 × 10–13, ΔR2 = 0.50%)
evidence: Statistical results including beta coefficients, t-values, p-values, and effect sizes are directly reported.

claim: The greatest effect sizes of the quadratic terms for cognition were observed for crystalized intelligence (β = –0.26, t = –6.87, p=6.7 × 10–12, ΔR2 = 0.43%).
source: For cognition, the greatest effect sizes of the quadratic terms were observed for total intelligence (β = –0.35, t = –7.45, p=1.0 × 10–13, ΔR2 = 0.50%) and crystalized intelligence (β = –0.26, t = –6.87, p=6.7 × 10–12, ΔR2 = 0.43%)
evidence: Statistical results including beta coefficients, t-values, p-values, and effect sizes are directly reported.

claim: The average breakpoint of the number of close friends for mental health and cognitive outcomes with significant quadratic terms was 4.89 ± 0.68.
source: The average breakpoint of the number of close friends for the mental health and cognitive outcomes with significant quadratic terms was 4.89 ± 0.68 (Figure 2h)
evidence: The breakpoint value is calculated from the two-lines test and reported with standard deviation.

claim: Both mental health and cognition were positively associated with close friend quantity, with an ideal number of around 5.
source: Both mental health and cognition were positively associated with close friend quantity, with an ideal number of around 5
evidence: This is a summary statement of the nonlinear association findings based on the breakpoint analysis.

claim: The nonlinear associations between close friend quantity and mental health/cognition were consistent in males and females.
source: These nonlinear associations were consistent in males and females (Figure 2—figure supplement 3)
evidence: Sex-stratified analyses are reported and referenced to supplementary figures.

claim: The number of same-sex close friends, but not of opposite-sex close friends, was significantly related to mental health and cognition (26 out of 30 measures with a significant F value after Bonferroni correction).
source: However, the number of same-sex close friends, but not of opposite-sex close friends, was significantly related to mental health and cognition (26 out of 30 measures with a significant F value after Bonferroni correction)
evidence: Statistical results from separate analyses of same-sex and opposite-sex friendships are reported.

claim: Children with 4.05 ± 0.59 same-sex close friends had the best mental health and cognitive functions.
source: children with 4.05 ± 0.59 same-sex close friends had the best mental health and cognitive functions (Figure 2—figure supplement 4)
evidence: The breakpoint for same-sex friendships is calculated and reported with standard deviation.

claim: The number of close friends was significantly associated with the total cortical area (F = 6.29, p=1.0 × 10–3).
source: In the ABCD study, the number of close friends was significantly associated with the total cortical area (F = 6.29, p=1.0 × 10–3; Figure 3d)
evidence: Statistical association between friendship quantity and brain structure is directly reported with F-value and p-value.

claim: The number of close friends was significantly associated with the total cortical volume (F = 5.80, p=3.1 × 10–3).
source: the number of close friends was significantly associated with the total cortical area (F = 6.29, p=1.0 × 10–3; Figure 3d), and the total cortical volume (F = 5.80, p=3.1 × 10–3)
evidence: Statistical association between friendship quantity and brain structure is directly reported with F-value and p-value.

claim: No significant relationship was found between the number of close friends and mean cortical thickness (F = 0.62, p=0.54).
source: No significant relationship between the number of close friends and mean cortical thickness (F = 0.62, p=0.54) and total subcortical volume (F = 3.94, p=0.02) was found
evidence: Null findings are reported with statistical values.

claim: No significant relationship was found between the number of close friends and total subcortical volume (F = 3.94, p=0.02).
source: No significant relationship between the number of close friends and mean cortical thickness (F = 0.62, p=0.54) and total subcortical volume (F = 3.94, p=0.02) was found
evidence: The p-value does not meet the significance threshold implied by the context of other findings.

claim: After FDR correction, the significant cortical areas associated with the number of close friends were mainly located in the OFC, insula, the ACC, the anterior temporal cortex, and the TPJ.
source: After false discovery rate (FDR) correction (q < 0.05), the significant cortical areas associated with the number of close friends were mainly located in the OFC, insula, the ACC, the anterior temporal cortex, and the TPJ (Figure 3a)
evidence: Brain regions showing significant associations are identified after statistical correction and visualized in figures.

claim: The brain region with the largest effect size for the linear term was the OFC (left medial OFC [area 11l and 13l] and lateral OFC [area 47m and 47s]).
source: The brain region with the largest effect size for the linear term was the OFC (left medial OFC [area 11l and 13l] and lateral OFC [area 47m and 47s])
evidence: Effect size analysis identifies the OFC as having the strongest linear association.

claim: The quadratic terms of the number of close friends for all significant cortical regions were significant.
source: The quadratic terms of the number of close friends for all these regions were significant (Figure 3b)
evidence: Statistical significance of quadratic terms is reported for all identified brain regions.

claim: The greatest effect sizes of quadratic terms for brain regions were observed in the temporal pole (left STGa: β = –0.58, t = –4.20, p=2.8 × 10–5, ΔR2 = 0.18%).
source: the greatest effect sizes were observed in the temporal pole (left STGa: β = –0.58, t = –4.20, p=2.8 × 10–5, ΔR2 = 0.18%, Figure 3e; right TGd: β = –3.32, t = –4.11, p=4.0 × 10–5, ΔR2 = 0.18%, Figure 3f)
evidence: Statistical results for specific brain regions are reported with beta coefficients, t-values, p-values, and effect sizes.

claim: The greatest effect sizes of quadratic terms for brain regions were observed in the temporal pole (right TGd: β = –3.32, t = –4.11, p=4.0 × 10–5, ΔR2 = 0.18%).
source: the greatest effect sizes were observed in the temporal pole (left STGa: β = –0.58, t = –4.20, p=2.8 × 10–5, ΔR2 = 0.18%, Figure 3e; right TGd: β = –3.32, t = –4.11, p=4.0 × 10–5, ΔR2 = 0.18%, Figure 3f)
evidence: Statistical results for specific brain regions are reported with beta coefficients, t-values, p-values, and effect sizes.

claim: Two-lines tests suggested that participants with around five close friends (breakpoint = 5.30 ± 0.85) had the largest areas in cortical regions.
source: Further, two-lines tests suggested that participants with around five close friends (breakpoint = 5.30 ± 0.85) had the largest areas in these cortical regions (Figure 3—figure supplement 4)
evidence: Breakpoint analysis results are reported with mean and standard deviation.

claim: The number of close friends was not related to cortical area in the >5 group.
source: However, the number of close friends was not related to cortical area in the >5 group (Figure 3—figure supplement 5d)
evidence: Null findings in the subgroup analysis are reported and referenced to figures.

claim: The cortical area associative patterns of close friend quantity in the ≤5 and >5 groups were not correlated (r = –0.02, p=0.78).
source: Moreover, the cortical area associative patterns of close friend quantity in the two groups were not correlated (r = –0.02, p=0.78; Figure 3—figure supplement 5e)
evidence: Correlation analysis between the two groups is reported with correlation coefficient and p-value.

claim: The correlations between the spatial pattern of cortical area related to the number of close friends and densities of neurotransmitters were not significant except for the μ-opioid receptor (Spearman's rho = 0.44, Bonferroni corrected pperm = 0.02).
source: We found that the correlations between the spatial pattern of cortical area related to the number of close friends and densities of neurotransmitters were not significant except for the μ-opioid receptor (Spearman's rho = 0.44, Bonferroni corrected pperm = 0.02; Figure 4a and b)
evidence: Spatial correlation analysis results are reported with statistical values and correction methods.

claim: OPRM1 gene expression was highly expressed in regions related to the number of close friends (Spearman's rho = 0.45, pperm = 0.001).
source: Transcriptomic analyses showed that OPRM1 (Spearman's rho = 0.45, pperm = 0.001; Figure 4c) and OPRK1 (Spearman's rho = 0.46, pperm = 0.002; Figure 4d) were highly expressed in regions related to the number of close friends
evidence: Gene expression analysis results are reported with correlation coefficients and permutation-based p-values.

claim: OPRK1 gene expression was highly expressed in regions related to the number of close friends (Spearman's rho = 0.46, pperm = 0.002).
source: Transcriptomic analyses showed that OPRM1 (Spearman's rho = 0.45, pperm = 0.001; Figure 4c) and OPRK1 (Spearman's rho = 0.46, pperm = 0.002; Figure 4d) were highly expressed in regions related to the number of close friends
evidence: Gene expression analysis results are reported with correlation coefficients and permutation-based p-values.

claim: Participants having closer to five close friends had fewer ADHD symptoms 2 years later (β = 0.04, p<0.001).
source: The cross-lagged panel model (CLPM) revealed that participants having closer to five close friends had fewer ADHD symptoms 2 y later (β = 0.04, p<0.001; Figure 5a)
evidence: Longitudinal analysis results from cross-lagged panel models are reported with standardized coefficients and p-values.

claim: More close friends contributed to fewer ADHD symptoms in the ≤5 group (β = –0.04, p=0.003).
source: CLPMs in separate groups confirmed that more close friends contributed to fewer ADHD symptoms in ≤5 group (β = –0.04, p=0.003; Figure 5—figure supplement 1a)
evidence: Subgroup longitudinal analysis results are reported with standardized coefficients and p-values.

claim: The effect of close friends on ADHD symptoms reversed in the >5 group (β = 0.05, p=0.019).
source: but the effect reversed in the >5 group (β = 0.05, p=0.019; Figure 5—figure supplement 1b)
evidence: Subgroup longitudinal analysis results showing opposite direction of effect are reported with standardized coefficients and p-values.

claim: The relationship between the absolute difference of close friend number to five and crystalized intelligence was bidirectional.
source: The relationship between the absolute difference of close friend number to five and crystalized intelligence was bidirectional (Figure 5b)
evidence: Cross-lagged panel model results showing bidirectional relationships are reported and visualized.

claim: Only in the ≤5 group was a significant negative correlation found between crystalized intelligence at baseline and the number of close friends at 2-year follow-up (β = –0.06, p=0.001).
source: Only in the ≤5 group was a significant negative correlation found between crystalized intelligence at baseline and the number of close friends at 2-year follow-up (β = –0.06, p=0.001; Figure 5—figure supplement 1c and d)
evidence: Subgroup longitudinal analysis results are reported with standardized coefficients and p-values.

claim: The total identified cortical area partly mediated the association between the number of close friends and ADHD symptoms (6.5%, 95% CI [3.4%, 14%]; path a*b: –0.005, 95% CI [-0.008,–0.003]).
source: The total identified cortical area partly mediated the association between the number of close friends and ADHD symptoms (6.5%, 95% CI [3.4%, 14%]; path a*b: –0.005, 95% CI [-0.008,–0.003]; Figure 5c)
evidence: Mediation analysis results are reported with percentage mediated, confidence intervals, and path coefficients.

claim: The mediation effects of individual significant brain regions on the association between close friends and ADHD symptoms ranged from 1.52 to 4.68%.
source: the mediation effects of individual significant regions ranged from 1.52 to 4.68% (Figure 5d)
evidence: Individual region mediation analysis results are reported with percentage ranges.

claim: The association between the number of close friends and crystalized intelligence was partly mediated by the total identified cortical area (13.5%, 95% CI [8.1%, 27%]; path a*b: 0.008, 95% CI [0.005, 0.01]).
source: Similarly, the association between the number of close friends and crystalized intelligence was partly mediated by the total identified cortical area (13.5%, 95% CI [8.1%, 27%]; path a*b: 0.008, 95% CI [0.005, 0.01]; Figure 5e)
evidence: Mediation analysis results are reported with percentage mediated, confidence intervals, and path coefficients.

claim: The mediation effects of individual significant brain regions on the association between close friends and crystalized intelligence ranged from 2.58 to 8.52%.
source: ranging from 2.58 to 8.52% for each significant region (Figure 5f)
evidence: Individual region mediation analysis results are reported with percentage ranges.

claim: Three indicators of friendship network size (indegree, outdegree, and reciprocal degree) were significantly related to well-being in the social network dataset.
source: Three indicators of friendship network size (i.e., outdegree, indegree, and reciprocal degree; Figure 6) were significantly related to well-being (indegree: F = 38.63, p=1.8 × 10–17; outdegree: F = 33.55, p=2.9 × 10–15; reciprocal degree: F = 53.87, p=4.8 × 10–24; Figure 6—figure supplement 1a)
evidence: Statistical associations in the independent dataset are reported with F-values and p-values.

claim: Three indicators of friendship network size (indegree, outdegree, and reciprocal degree) were significantly related to GPA in the social network dataset.
source: Three indicators of friendship network size (i.e., outdegree, indegree, and reciprocal degree; Figure 6) were significantly related to well-being (indegree: F = 38.63, p=1.8 × 10–17; outdegree: F = 33.55, p=2.9 × 10–15; reciprocal degree: F = 53.87, p=4.8 × 10–24; Figure 6—figure supplement 1a) and GPA (indegree: F = 28.08, p=6.7×10–13; outdegree: F = 46.66, p=6.2 × 10–21; reciprocal degree: F = 192.65, p=2.1 × 10–83; Figure 6—figure supplement 1b)
evidence: Statistical associations in the independent dataset are reported with F-values and p-values.

claim: For well-being, only the quadratic term of outdegree was significant after Bonferroni correction (β = –2.9 × 10–4, t = –3.67, p=2.4 × 10–4, ΔR2 = 0.07%).
source: Specifically, for well-being, all linear terms were significant, but only the quadratic term of outdegree was significant after Bonferroni correction (β = –2.9 × 10–4, t = –3.67, p=2.4 × 10–4, ΔR2 = 0.07%; Figure 6—figure supplement 1c)
evidence: Statistical results for quadratic terms are reported with beta coefficients, t-values, p-values, and effect sizes.

claim: For GPA, the quadratic terms of all three friendship network indicators were significant, with the greatest effect size observed in outdegree (β = –0.001, t = –6.02, p=1.8 × 10–9, ΔR2 = 0.17%).
source: For GPA, the quadratic terms of all three indicators were significant, and the greatest effect size was observed in the outdegree (β = –0.001, t = –6.02, p=1.8 × 10–9, ΔR2 = 0.17%; Figure 6—figure supplement 1d)
evidence: Statistical results for quadratic terms are reported with beta coefficients, t-values, p-values, and effect sizes.

claim: The positive association of outdegree with well-being and GPA diminished once the outward nomination reached 7 or 8.
source: The two-lines tests revealed that the positive association of outdegree with well-being and GPA diminished once the outward nomination reached 7 or 8 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1d)
evidence: Breakpoint analysis results from two-lines tests are reported.

claim: Late childhood and its transition toward adolescence is a period marked by decreasing parental influence alongside increasing peer influence.
source: Late childhood and its transition toward adolescence is a period marked by decreasing parental influence alongside increasing peer influence
evidence: This is a general statement about developmental psychology that is widely accepted in the field.

claim: Late childhood is a period critical for social interaction, during which friendships are especially important.
source: It is a period critical for social interaction, during which friendships are especially important (Blakemore and Mills, 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: During late childhood, the social brain is still undergoing significant development, in parallel with changes in social cognition.
source: During this period, the social brain is still undergoing significant development, in parallel with changes in social cognition (Mills et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research on brain development.

claim: Psychiatric disorders often have an onset in adolescence.
source: Meanwhile, evidence suggests that psychiatric disorders often have an onset in adolescence (Kessler et al., 2005)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to epidemiological research.

claim: Psychiatric disorder onset in adolescence may be partly influenced by concurrent changes in the social environment and brain.
source: which may be partly influenced by the concurrent changes in the social environment and brain (Paus et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and represents an inference about causal mechanisms.

claim: Positive social relationships such as close friendships are essential for mental health and cognition in children and adolescents.
source: It has been well established that positive social relationships such as close friendships are essential for mental health and cognition in children and adolescents (Marion et al., 2013; Narr et al., 2019; Wentzel et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: It remains unclear whether having more close friends is necessarily better.
source: However, it remains unclear whether having more close friends is necessarily better
evidence: This identifies a gap in the literature that the study aims to address.

claim: Cognitive constraints and time resources limit the number of close social ties that an individual can maintain simultaneously.
source: Cognitive constraints and time resources limit the number of close social ties that an individual can maintain simultaneously (Dunbar, 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dunbar's social brain hypothesis.

claim: The innermost layer of the friendship group with the highest emotional closeness is around five close friends (the so-called Dunbar's number).
source: The innermost layer of the friendship group with the highest emotional closeness is around five close friends (the so-called Dunbar's number) (Zhou et al., 2005)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to research on social network structure.

claim: A large study of a nationally representative sample in the United States reported that adolescents with either too many or too few friends had higher levels of depressive symptoms.
source: For instance, a large study of a nationally representative sample in the United States reported that adolescents with either too many or too few friends had higher levels of depressive symptoms (Falci and McNeely, 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Two large-scale studies reported that the benefits of social interactions for well-being were nearly negligible once the quantity reached a moderate level.
source: Two large-scale studies reported that the benefits of social interactions for well-being were nearly negligible once the quantity reached a moderate level (Kushlev et al., 2018; Ren et al., 2022)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A significant U-shaped effect was detected between positive relations with others and cognitive performance.
source: Additionally, a significant U-shaped effect was detected between positive relations with others and cognitive performance (Brown et al., 2021)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The assumption of linearity still dominates studies of social relationships.
source: Overall, the assumption of linearity still dominates studies of social relationships, and the effect of the friendship network size at the high end remains largely unexplored
evidence: This is a characterization of the current state of the literature.

claim: The social brain hypothesis proposes that the evolution of brain size is driven by complex social selection pressures.
source: The social brain hypothesis proposes that the evolution of brain size is driven by complex social selection pressures (Dunbar and Shultz, 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the foundational work on the social brain hypothesis.

claim: Animal studies have shown that social network size can predict the volume of the mid-superior temporal sulcus.
source: Animal studies have shown that social network size can predict the volume of the mid-superior temporal sulcus (Sallet et al., 2011; Testard et al., 2022)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to animal research.

claim: Neurons in the mid-superior temporal sulcus respond to socially relevant stimuli such as face expression and head movement to make or break social contact.
source: a region in which neurons respond to socially relevant stimuli such as face expression and head movement to make or break social contact (Hasselmo et al., 1989a; Hasselmo et al., 1989b)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to neurophysiological research.

claim: Several key brain regions, including the medial prefrontal cortex, the cortex in the superior temporal sulcus, the temporoparietal junction, amygdala, and the anterior insula, have been implicated in social cognitive processes.
source: In human neuroimaging studies, several key brain regions, including the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC, i.e. orbitofrontal [OFC] and anterior cingulate cortex [ACC]), the cortex in the superior temporal sulcus (STS), the temporoparietal junction (TPJ), amygdala, and the anterior insula, have been implicated in social cognitive processes (Frith and Frith, 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review of human neuroimaging research.

claim: There has been an increasing number of studies dedicated to investigating the social brain in children and adolescents over the past decade.
source: Moreover, there has been an increasing number of studies dedicated to investigating the social brain in children and adolescents over the past decade (Andrews et al., 2021; Burnett et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent research.

claim: The μ-opioid receptor is widely distributed in the brain, particularly in regions associated with social pain such as the ACC and anterior insula.
source: At the molecular level, the μ-opioid receptor is widely distributed in the brain, particularly in regions associated with social pain such as the ACC and anterior insula (Baumgärtner et al., 2006)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to neuroimaging research on receptor distribution.

claim: Recent studies have identified the crucial role of μ-opioid receptors in forming and maintaining friendships.
source: Recent studies have identified the crucial role of μ-opioid receptors in forming and maintaining friendships (Dunbar, 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to recent research.

claim: Variations in the μ-opioid receptor gene have been related to individual differences in rejection sensitivity.
source: variations in the μ-opioid receptor gene have been related to individual differences in rejection sensitivity (Way et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to genetic research.

claim: Other neurotransmitters, including dopamine, serotonin, GABA, and noradrenaline, may interact with the opioids and are involved in social affiliation and social behavior.
source: In addition, other neurotransmitters, including dopamine, serotonin, GABA, and noradrenaline, may interact with the opioids, and are involved in social affiliation and social behavior (Machin and Dunbar, 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to research on neurotransmitter systems.

claim: Dysregulation of the social brain and neurotransmitter systems is implicated in the pathophysiology of major psychiatric disorders.
source: Dysregulation of the social brain and neurotransmitter systems is also implicated in the pathophysiology of major psychiatric disorders (Porcelli et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to research on psychiatric disorders.

claim: Changes in the social brain might explain the relationship between social connections and mental health.
source: Taken together, it is suggested that changes in the social brain might explain the relationship between social connections and mental health (Lamblin et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and represents a theoretical inference.

claim: The empirical evidence on the relationship between social brain changes and mental health is limited in late childhood and adolescence.
source: However, the empirical evidence on this topic is limited in late childhood and adolescence
evidence: This identifies a gap in the literature.

claim: The ABCD study is tracking the brain development and health of a nationally representative sample of children aged 9–11 years from 21 centers throughout the United States.
source: The ABCD study is tracking the brain development and health of a nationally representative sample of children aged 9–11 y from 21 centers throughout the United States (https://abcdstudy.org)
evidence: This describes the ABCD study design and is a factual statement about the dataset.

claim: Research protocols for the ABCD study were approved by the institutional review board of the University of California, San Diego (no. 160091), and the institutional review boards of the 21 data collection sites.
source: Research protocols were approved by the institutional review board of the University of California, San Diego (no. 160091), and the institutional review boards of the 21 data collection sites (Auchter et al., 2018)
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval supported by a citation.

claim: The Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL) has high inter-interviewer reliability, test–retest reliability, internal consistency, and criterion validity.
source: The CBCL has high inter-interviewer reliability, test–retest reliability, internal consistency, and criterion validity, and therefore is widely utilized by child psychiatrists, developmental psychologists, and other mental health professionals for clinical and research purposes (Achenbach et al., 1987)
evidence: This claim about the psychometric properties of the CBCL is supported by a citation.

claim: The NIH Toolbox has good reliability and validity in children.
source: Cognitive functions were assessed by the NIH Toolbox (Luciana et al., 2018), which has good reliability and validity in children (Akshoomoff et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim about the psychometric properties of the NIH Toolbox is supported by citations.

claim: The social network experiment was conducted among students in 56 middle schools in New Jersey, USA.
source: In order to extend the findings in the ABCD study, we utilized a publicly available dataset of a social network experiment, conducted among students in 56 middle schools in New Jersey, USA (Paluck et al., 2016)
evidence: This describes the social network dataset and is supported by a citation.

claim: The research protocol for the social network study was approved by the Princeton University Institutional Review Board.
source: All parents and students provided informed consent for the survey, and the research protocol was approved by the Princeton University Institutional Review Board
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: 3D T1- and T2-weighted structural images were collected using 3T scanners at 21 data collecting sites in the ABCD study.
source: In the ABCD study, 3D T1- and T2-weighted structural images were collected using 3T scanners at 21 data collecting sites (Casey et al., 2018)
evidence: This describes the MRI data collection protocol and is supported by a citation.

claim: FreeSurfer v6.0 was used to preprocess the structural MRI images in the ABCD study.
source: In brief, we used FreeSurfer v6.0 to preprocess the minimal preprocessed T1- and T2-weighted images downloaded from the ABCD study
evidence: This describes the image processing methods used.

claim: The cortical surface of each subject was parcellated into 180 cortical regions per hemisphere as defined in the Human Connectome Project multimodal parcellation (HCP-MMP) atlas.
source: Then, the cortical surface of each subject was registered to a standard fsaverage space and parcellated into 180 cortical regions per hemisphere as defined in the Human Connectome Project multimodal parcellation (HCP-MMP) atlas (Glasser et al., 2016)
evidence: This describes the brain parcellation method and is supported by a citation.

claim: Fourteen receptors and transporters across eight different neurotransmitter systems were investigated.
source: Fourteen receptors and transporters across eight different neurotransmitter systems (serotonin: 5HT1a, 5HT1b, 5HT2a, 5HT4, and 5HTT; dopamine: D1, D2, and DAT; GABA: GABAa; glutamate: mGluR5; norepinephrine: NAT; cannabinoid: CB1; opioid: MOR; acetylcholine: VAChT) were investigated
